source: Fu et al. (2022) Complexity-Based Prompting for Multi-Step Reasoning
finding: Worked examples with more reasoning steps beat simple ones as in-context demos. Complex demos beat hand-written and random demos on GSM8K.
numbers: Codex GSM8K: handcrafted 61.0, random 60.4, complex 66.6 (+5.6). text-davinci-002 GSM8K: 48.1, 49.7, 55.4 (+7.3). Greedy-decoding ablation chain on a GSM8K validation subset: original CoT 48.5, add 'think step by step' 54.0, complex prompt 58.0.
limits: Eight demos only; 2022-era models; validation subset small. Complexity measured as step count of the gold solution, not quality.
agent_relevance: Store the longer, fully-stepped version of a solved subgoal, not a terse one. Element-interactivity analogue: the human lit says complex examples suit capable learners.

source: Fu et al. (2022) Complexity-Based Prompting for Multi-Step Reasoning (selection schemes)
finding: A fixed set of 8 complex demos matched or beat retrieval by similarity on two of three datasets. Retrieval won on MathQA, where test items nearly duplicate training items.
numbers: Validation accuracy, random / centroid / retrieval (10,000 annotations) / complexity (8): GSM8K 52.5/52.0/56.0/58.5; MultiArith 86.5/92.0/88.0/93.0; MathQA 33.0/32.0/69.5/42.5.
limits: Retrieval cost scales with test set. MathQA retrieval gain comes from near-duplicate questions (apple/banana swaps), i.e. surface similarity, not structure.
agent_relevance: A subgoal library with similarity lookup will look great on templated benchmarks and less great on novel items. Report the near-duplicate rate.

source: Fu et al. (2022) Complexity-Based Prompting for Multi-Step Reasoning (direction of generalization)
finding: Complex demos did not help most on hard items. They matched simple demos on hard items and gained on easier items. Gains held with noisy and transferred prompts.
numbers: On GSM8K simple prompts did better on items of 3 steps or fewer in one panel; complex did better on longer items. Trend 'more steps, higher accuracy' held in-distribution, noisy-labelled (MathQA) and transferred (GSM8K prompts to MultiArith) except one MultiArith case.
limits: Reading the figure, not a table. Single model family.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a rich example only helps hard problems. Test it across difficulty strata.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models (ICLR)
finding: Showing the decomposition into subproblems in the demo gives huge gains on length generalization and small gains on GSM8K. The gain grows with the number of steps.
numbers: SCAN length split: 99.7 with least-to-most vs about 16 for the other prompts (code-davinci-002; rows 16.7/16.2/99.7). GSM8K 62.39 vs CoT 60.87 (text elsewhere says 60.97). By steps: 5+ steps 45.23 vs 39.07; 2 steps 74.53 vs 76.68 (CoT better). DROP non-football 82.45 vs 74.77, football 73.42 vs 59.56.
limits: One model (code-davinci-002). Paper says almost every GSM8K failure of LtM is a wrong decomposition or wrong solve step, so the gain is capped by the decomposer. Inconsistent CoT figure in the text.
agent_relevance: Subgoal decomposition helps most on long chains and can lose on short ones. Add a gate by expected step count.

source: Zhang et al. (2022) Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models
finding: Auto-generated worked solutions can match hand-written ones if the example set is diverse. Picking demos by similarity makes the model copy the same mistake.
numbers: MultiArith: Manual-CoT 91.7, Auto-CoT 92.0, Zero-Shot-CoT 78.7. GSM8K: 46.9, 47.9, 40.7. Zero-shot errors 128/600 (21.3%). Of those, still unresolved: Retrieval-Q-CoT 46.9% vs Random-Q-CoT 25.8%.
limits: GPT-3 175B, 2022. Auto-CoT also used heuristics to drop long wrong rationales. Wrong-demo test on MultiArith only.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of a bad stored subgoal solution: nearest-neighbour retrieval of an unverified case propagates its error. Verify before store; keep diversity.

source: Zhang et al. (2022) Auto-CoT, robustness to wrong demonstrations
finding: Diversity-based sampling tolerated up to 50 percent wrong demonstrations without large loss; sampling within one cluster did not.
numbers: MultiArith with 0 to 50 percent wrong demos: Auto-CoT 'does not degrade significantly'; In-Cluster Sampling degrades. Paper claim: one or two wrong demos out of 8 do not hurt.
limits: Figure-based, no table of values. Old models. Conflicts with later work where wrong demos hurt reasoning-tuned models (see A05.01 d12, d13).
agent_relevance: Break-even wrong share depends on diversity of the set. Needs a measurement for our agent.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Teaching Algorithmic Reasoning via In-context Learning
finding: Fully explicit, unambiguous step-by-step worked examples teach an algorithm in context and generalise to longer inputs. Vague steps do not.
numbers: Table 2 (algorithmic prompt vs best baseline): addition length 19: 90.5% vs 9.5%; subtraction 14: 65.6% vs 16.7%; multiplication 7: 79.7% vs 5.5%; parity 20: 95.0% vs 50.0%.
limits: Arithmetic and parity, not open maths. Long prompts. 2022 PaLM-class model. 'Error reduction 10x' is on near-zero baselines.
agent_relevance: Worked examples must be fully explicit (no skipped carry, no hidden indexing). A 'solution sketch' entry will teach less than a complete one.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Algorithmic prompting, ablations and error injection
finding: The model follows the example rather than only copying format. Systematic errors in every example step drove accuracy to near 0%. Irregular errors in a subset cost little.
numbers: Addition: irregular errors in prompt, small degradation; systematic errors, accuracy near 0%. Every correct final answer had all intermediate steps correct. Removing explicit carry equation or using variable-position indexing lowered accuracy (Fig 3a).
limits: Contrasts with Min et al. (2022) where shuffled labels barely matter for simple tasks. Task here needs the rule; there the model already knew it.
agent_relevance: Support for the rule: wrong content in a worked example matters when the task needs the example's rule. Gate on whether the class needs the stored procedure.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Algorithmic prompting as tool use for GSM8K
finding: Putting an addition algorithm example in context raised GSM8K when it was called as a tool, but logic accuracy fell from interference.
numbers: Chain-of-thought with algo call: overall 55.8%, logical accuracy 57.7%, addition accuracy 98.4%. Without: overall 27.4%, logical 70.6%, addition 61.9%.
limits: Subset setup in the paper; one model. Interference cost is real: logic accuracy dropped 12.9 points.
agent_relevance: Adding a procedure example can hurt other steps. Track side effects on the rest of the chain.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: An Exploration in Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: Labelling training problems with skills, then showing solved exemplars that match the skill the model names, beats random, topic-based and complex-CoT exemplars on MATH.
numbers: MATH, GPT-4-0613: CoT 42.2; Complex CoT 50.30; CoT+Topic-Based 50.31; CoT+Skill-Based 53.88 (+11.6 over CoT; +3.5 over Complex CoT and Topic). Per topic e.g. Algebra 73.12, Geometry 41.75, Number theory 51.10.
limits: Skill labels made by GPT-4 on the training set; 117 skills for MATH. Preprint, under review. The same model both picks the skill and solves.
agent_relevance: This is nearly our subgoal library: label, cluster, retrieve solved exemplars by skill. Direct evidence the label-first step beats topic or random retrieval.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024), GSM8K and transfer
finding: On a near-ceiling model the gain on GSM8K is small. Random exemplars gave nothing. Skill exemplars helped a weaker model more.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-4-0613: CoT 93.00; CoT+Random 92.87; CoT+Skill 94.31; with maj@5 95.38. GPT-3.5-Turbo: Retrieval-RSD 76.8 vs Skill-Based 82.03.
limits: 1.3-point gain on a model near ceiling; one run each, no intervals reported in the text read. Gains also reported when exemplars transferred to weaker models (Tables 5-6).
agent_relevance: Matches the human pattern: worked examples help most where the learner has the most to learn; near ceiling there is no room.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Skills-in-Context: Unlocking Compositionality in Large Language Models
finding: Putting the skill definitions and worked compositional examples that cite those skills in the same prompt gives near-perfect generalisation to harder items. Both parts are needed.
numbers: Dynamic programming (8 numbers), ChatGPT: CoT 72.0; SKiC 98.0; minus skill text 94.0; minus skill grounding in steps 82.0. GSM8K ChatGPT over three exemplar orders: CoT 73.0-74.4, SKiC 86.9-87.8. MATH GPT-4: SKiC 56.4 vs ComplexCoT 50.3.
limits: Hand-built or semi-automatic skills. GPT-4 internal-skill activation rate on MATH is 24.3 percent: most gain is not from the supplied skills. ChatGPT MATH 40.6 (skills from ChatGPT) vs 38.9 (from GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Library entries should name the skill and show it being used in a worked case, in the same prompt. Skill text alone or example alone is weaker.

source: Chen et al. (2024) SKiC, cross-task transfer and error profile
finding: A GSM8K prompt applied unchanged to MATH and FOLIO transferred better with skills. Most remaining errors came from skills missing in the prompt.
numbers: ChatGPT, GSM8K-designed prompts applied to MATH: CoT 28.2, SKiC 31.34; FOLIO 68.8 vs 72.5. Error analysis on 50 failures per task: most common error is unseen basic skills; incorrect composition dominates GSM8K.
limits: Small transfer margins (+3.1 on MATH). Error analysis uses 50 cases per task, hand coded.
agent_relevance: Coverage of the library matters more than polish: missing subgoal was the top failure.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: A worked example that itself contains an irrelevant sentence, and an explicit 'ignore irrelevant information' line, both make models more robust. Example content shapes what the model attends to.
numbers: code-davinci-002 on GSM-IC-4K, CoT micro accuracy 72.4 (exemplars clean); with instruction 77.8; with irrelevant-context exemplars 76.8. Macro accuracy CoT 6.0 with clean exemplars; 14.0 with irrelevant-context exemplars. LtM macro 18.0 to 28.0 with such exemplars. Best macro with self-consistency: 45%.
limits: Synthetic distractors; 2022-2023 models. Macro accuracy (all variants of a problem right) stays low for every method.
agent_relevance: Worked cases should show the filtering step, not only the clean path. Stored cases drawn from clean benchmarks may lack it.

source: Morrison, Margulieux and Decker (talk, 2020) Using Subgoal Labels to Reduce Cognitive Load in Introductory Programming (slides)
finding: Subgoal-labelled worked examples beat plain worked examples in a large CS1 course. The slides give the effect size only as medium (quizzes) and small (exam total).
numbers: University course, N = 307, Fall 2018, same instructors, quizzes, exams. Quizzes: medium effect for average and total. Exams: small effect for total, no difference for average exam score. At-risk subgroup, expected difficulty: exam average 74% subgoal vs 67% control. Half as likely to withdraw or fail.
limits: Slide deck, not the paper; no d values. Quasi-experimental by semester, not randomised. Authors' own cited prior work lists the same group's earlier studies (2012-2016).
agent_relevance: Subgoal labels are the human version of our library's key. Gains concentrated in low-prior-knowledge learners, consistent with expertise reversal.

source: Morrison, Margulieux and Decker (2020) The curious case of loops. Computer Science Education 30(2)
finding: Pooled three studies in three populations. Subgoal labels helped, but only in two arrangements. The effect was described as stable but the abstract gives no number.
numbers: Two conditions did best: given labels with a far gap between examples and practice problems, and self-written labels with a near gap. Three studies pooled; effect size 'medium-large' per search summary.
limits: Abstract page only; no effect size on the page. The pattern depends on transfer distance, so it is a boundary condition.
agent_relevance: Who writes the label and how far the target is from the example both change the result. Let the agent write its own labels for near targets; store given labels for far ones.

source: Morrison et al. (2019-2020) subgoal labelling replication at a second institution (search summary)
finding: A replication with a new population and institution is reported under the title 'Learning loops: a replication study illuminates impact of HS courses'. Not read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only the search summary was seen; the PDF links were blocked. Do not cite figures from it.
agent_relevance: Marks where a failed or conditional replication would be found.

source: Margulieux, Catrambone and Schaeffer (2018) subgoal-labelled expository text across domains (search summary)
finding: Labelled worked examples consistently improved problem solving, but labelled expository text had a different pattern in each of three domains.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Search snippet only. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Labels on solved cases are the safer bet than labels on general text.

source: What Works Clearinghouse (2015) record of Booth et al., Design-based research within the constraints of practice: AlgebraByExample
finding: A randomised classroom trial of worked examples in algebra homework found small positive gains on all three algebra measures. The WWC rated it 'meets standards with reservations' and its means are close.
numbers: 380 students, 25 classrooms (189 intervention, 191 comparison). Means intervention vs comparison: state-test items 0.49 vs 0.48 (improvement index 15); conceptual 0.51 vs 0.49 (11); procedural 0.25 vs 0.25 (10). Page says all three significant.
limits: Means are nearly equal while the improvement index is large, and procedural means are identical but marked significant: internal inconsistency on the WWC page. Search summary wrongly called the means effect sizes. No Hedges g on the page. Not a main finding for WWC (supplemental).
agent_relevance: A realistic size for the worked-example effect in classrooms is small. Do not plan on the lab-sized effects.

source: SERP Institute, AlgebraByExample research summary
finding: The programme reports gains in percentage points, not effect sizes, and the page lists no null results.
numbers: Struggling students: +10 points conceptual knowledge over a year, same teacher control; all students +4 points procedural while solving half as many problems; +7 points on released state test items. 'Over 300 classrooms, more than 130 teachers and 6,000 students' (not tied to one study).
limits: Developer's own page; no sample per result; outcome not in effect size; no mention of null studies. Publication-bias risk.
agent_relevance: Same size story as the WWC page: modest, mainly efficiency (half the problems for the same or better score).

source: Kapur, Hattie, Grossman and Sinha (2022) Fail, flip, fix, and feed. Frontiers in Education
finding: Rival to worked-example-first: problem solving before instruction. The authors report it beats instruction-first on average and add a caution that bias-adjusted estimates are larger.
numbers: Cites Sinha and Kapur (2021): 53 studies, 166 comparisons, Hedges g 0.36 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.51). Higher fidelity to productive-failure design: g 0.37 to 0.58. After publication-bias adjustment g 0.87. The paper's own flipped-learning meta-analysis covers 173 studies.
limits: Secondary citation of the 2021 meta-analysis; the comparison group is traditional instruction, not worked examples. Authors are the productive-failure group (allegiance). Not a test against worked examples.
agent_relevance: Rival theory. It predicts the opposite order for novel-concept learning. Our agent: attempt first then see the case (S5 after failure) is the PS-I analogue.

source: Sinha and Kapur (2021) When problem solving followed by instruction works. Rev Educ Res 91(5) (search summary)
finding: Meta-analysis of problem-solving-first against instruction-first. Not read directly; the publisher page was blocked (403).
numbers: As reported in b21: g 0.36 [0.20, 0.51], 53 studies, 166 comparisons; bias-adjusted g 0.87. Search summary says younger learners (grades 2-5) and domain-general skills favoured instruction first.
limits: Search summary only for the moderators. Treat the moderator claim as unverified.
agent_relevance: The grade 2-5 and domain-general exceptions match the worked-example boundary: low prior knowledge favours more guidance.

source: Barbieri, Miller-Cotto, Clerjuste and Chawla (2023) Meta-analysis of worked examples in mathematics. Educ Psych Rev (search summary)
finding: Pooled effect of worked examples on maths was medium. Correct-only examples beat incorrect-only and mixed sets. Self-explanation prompts lowered the effect.
numbers: g = 0.48 (43 articles, 55 studies, 181 effect sizes; confirmed in A05.01 critique). Correct-only larger than incorrect-only or mixed (search summary).
limits: Springer PDF blocked in this session; numbers come from the earlier A05.01 audit and a search summary. Not re-opened here.
agent_relevance: Anchor for the size. Do not add self-explanation as a default; see the self-explanation subfield.

source: van Loon-Hillen, van Gog and Brand-Gruwel (search summary) primary school maths, worked examples vs practice
finding: A quasi-experiment found no test-score difference and no cognitive-load difference, but worked-example pupils needed less study time.
numbers: Not read; only 'no significant differences in test performance or cognitive load; significantly less acquisition time' was seen.
limits: Search snippet only; the DOI in the link may not match the paper. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Efficiency without a score gain is the most common outcome. Count tokens saved, not only accuracy.

source: Own synthesis (this run): LLM exemplar studies versus human worked-example moderators
finding: Across the seven LLM papers read here, the winning exemplar choice is one that matches the needed skill, is complete and correct, and is diverse. Similarity alone is unreliable.
numbers: Skill-matched exemplars +3.5 over topic-matched on MATH (Didolkar); similarity retrieval 46.9% vs diverse 25.8% unresolved (Zhang); retrieval beat complexity only on near-duplicate MathQA (Fu).
limits: Synthesis of opened sources; mixed models (2022 to 2024) and mixed metrics; no equal-token comparison in any of them.
agent_relevance: Rule for the library: key by skill label, require complete verified solutions, add diversity, and test against a similarity-only arm.

source: Own synthesis (this run): discriminating tests between worked-example-first and problem-first
finding: The two theories diverge on learner prior knowledge and on whether the target is a new concept or a routine procedure. Worked examples are predicted to win on routine procedures for novices; problem-first on conceptual novelty with some prior knowledge.
numbers: From b21 (g 0.36 problem-first; grade 2-5 exceptions) and WWC/SERP (algebra procedure, efficiency). No single experiment in this set compares both on the same items.
limits: No head-to-head study opened. The two literatures use different tests (procedural transfer vs conceptual).
agent_relevance: Our agent: for known procedure classes, show the case first. For new structure, let it try first and show the case after a failed attempt.
